result.summary: Pindar celebrates Chromios of Aitna for a chariot victory won at Sikyon. He recounts how Adrastos founded the Sikyonian games and the doomed expedition of the Seven against Thebes, then praises Chromios's war record and fortune.

scenes.title: Editor's introduction
scenes.summary: The editor explains that the victory was won at Sikyon, not Nemea, and that the date is uncertain.

scenes.title: Procession to Aitna
scenes.summary: The singers lead the victory song from Sikyon to Aitna and the house of Chromios, and recall Adrastos's founding of the games.

scenes.title: Adrastos and the Seven
scenes.summary: Adrastos flees Argos, is reconciled with Amphiaraos through Eriphyle, and leads the doomed expedition against Thebes, where Amphiaraos is swallowed by the earth.
scenes.stakes: Adrastos and his army face death after ignoring Zeus's warning signs at Thebes.

scenes.title: Prayer and praise of Chromios
scenes.summary: Pindar prays Zeus for good laws for Aitna and praises Chromios's courage in war by land and sea.
scenes.stakes: Aitna's peace is threatened by Phoenician (Carthaginian) war.

scenes.title: Banquet and closing boast
scenes.summary: Pindar speaks of calm old age, calls for wine in the victory goblets, and claims his song hits the Muses' mark.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim that even sons of gods flee divine terror.
Pindar's proud closing boast about his poetry.

analysis.text: The ode pairs athletic honour with the myth of Adrastos, warning that success needs the gods' favour.
Chromios served Hieron of Syracuse, and the Phoenician reference reflects Sicilian Greeks' fear of Carthage.

fun_facts.text: Though grouped with the Nemeans, this ode celebrates a victory at Sikyon's local Pythian games.

language_notes.text: Aitna was a new city founded by Hieron; 'invading guests' is a playful phrase for the crowd of visitors that fills Chromios's open doors.
The mother and her twin children are Leto, Apollo and Artemis, who share guardianship of Pytho (Delphi).
'Withal' means 'also' or 'in addition'; 'voiceful' means loud and resounding.
Eriphyle, sister of Adrastos, was given as wife to Amphiaraos, son of Oikleus, to end their feud. She later betrayed him, which is why she is called his slayer.
The expedition of the Seven against Thebes is the well-known legend. Zeus (the son of Kronos) sent lightning as a warning sign against it.
'Fed the white smoke with their bodies' means their corpses were burned on funeral pyres.
Amphiaraos was saved from death in flight by Zeus, who opened the earth for him. Periklymenos was a Theban warrior who would have speared him in the back.
Phenician spears refer to the Carthaginians, Phoenician colonists in the west, who threatened Greek Sicily. Pindar hopes the battle with them can be postponed.
"Would fain defer unto the utmost" means he would gladly put off the conflict as long as possible.
Enyalios is a war-god, here often identified with Ares or his aspect; "havoc of Enyalios" means the destruction of battle.
Hektor was the Trojan champion, famed beside the river Skamander. Pindar compares Chromios's glory at the Heloros to him.
"The grapes' potent child" is a poetic way of saying wine.
"Leto's son" is Apollo; the crowns suggest the goblets were prizes won at games in his honour, sent from Sikyon.
The Charites are the Graces, goddesses of charm and beauty who favoured poets.

context_notes.text: Chromios was a Sicilian commander and brother-in-law of Hieron, tyrant of Syracuse, and is also honoured in Nemean 1.
Adrastos, king of Sikyon, was said to have founded the games there in honour of Apollo (Phoibos). The Asopos is a river near Sikyon.
Adrastos, son of Talaos, fled Argos after a quarrel with Amphiaraos and became king at Sikyon.
Aitna was a Sicilian city founded by Hieron of Syracuse. Chromios was a commander closely tied to Hieron.
Sikyon, a city in the Peloponnese, held games where Chromios's mares won a chariot victory, with silver cups as prizes.

literary_notes.text: The games are called the 'crown' of all horse contests, picturing the event as the finest ornament or highest prize.
The earth cleaving 'deep-breasted' and swallowing the hero with his horses gives a vivid, almost bodily picture of divine rescue.
The closing maxim turns the myth into a general truth about terror from the gods, which even divine offspring flee.
Old age is imagined as a ripening crop, and the calm day as its harvest, rewarding righteous toil in youth.
The mountain-top image suggests there is no higher peak of human happiness than Chromios's wealth joined with fame.
The banquet "loveth peace" and the singer's voice "waxeth brave", giving feast and song lively human traits.
Pindar likens his song to a javelin thrown at a target, claiming his praise lands closest to the Muses' mark.
